clue.text: See 23
These glands are female, all the same?

parts.note: read as nothing (the letter for zero) plus a verb meaning differs, the answer says nothing differs, which is to say all the same

explanation.surface: A question about whether female glands are all identical.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: split (1,6), O for nothing plus VARIES reads as nothing varies, i.e. all the same; the question mark flags the backwards reading.
explanation.definitionFit: The ovaries are the egg-producing glands of the female reproductive system.

clue.text: Something that is tripped switches characteristic of laser shows?

indicators.note: switches tells us to swap the order of the two words in the phrase that follows

parts.note: a laser show puts on a fantastic light display

explanation.surface: Something tripped, like a switch, at a dazzling laser show.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'trip the light fantastic' is an old idiom meaning to dance; the light fantastic is the thing tripped. 'Switches' looks like light switches but signals swapping FANTASTIC LIGHT round.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'trip the light fantastic', meaning to dance, makes the light fantastic the object one trips.

clue.text: Consumption: a single steak

parts.note: consumption is an old name for tuberculosis, TB
a single means one

explanation.surface: A diner's note: eating just one steak.
explanation.definitionFit: A T-bone is a cut of beef steak with a T-shaped bone.

clue.text: The ever-expanding Carlsberg Corporation?

parts.note: corporation is an old jokey word for a paunch, and Carlsberg is a lager, so a lager-fed growing paunch

explanation.surface: A brewing giant that keeps growing its business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corporation' is an old humorous term for a large belly; Carlsberg stands for beer in general.
explanation.definitionFit: A paunch built up by drinking lager keeps growing, the ever-swelling belly of a heavy drinker.

clue.text: Previously underemployed in year, sly one viewed topless women

indicators.note: seen topless, each of the four words in, year, sly and one is shown without its first letter

explanation.surface: A seedy tale of a sly man ogling topless women in a lean year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'viewed topless' strips the heads from 'in year sly one', leaving N EAR LY NE.
explanation.definitionFit: Second-hand goods described as barely used have seen little service before, hardly worked by their previous owner.

clue.text: Flirt with Bill's partner — not me, sad to admit

indicators.note: to admit means to let something in, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: lovers bill and coo, so coo partners bill

indicators.note: sad as in sorry or in a bad way, so the letters of not me are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone sheepishly admits it was not they who flirted with Bill's partner.
explanation.walkthrough: Lovers are said to bill and coo, so coo is the partner of bill. The anagram of NOT ME goes inside after the first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To come on to someone is an idiom for making sexual advances, i.e. flirting with them.

clue.text: Case of correspondence between London and Washington?

definitions.text: Case of correspondence between London and Washington?

parts.words: Case of correspondence between London and Washington?
parts.note: upper-case letters are called capitals, and mail sent between two capital cities is literally capital post

explanation.surface: A diplomatic matter of letters exchanged between Britain and America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' is not a legal case or a bag but the printer's sense, upper case.
explanation.definitionFit: Upper-case characters are known as capitals, and letters posted between national capitals fit the same phrase.

clue.text: Heavyweight mixing it a bit with 12 urbanite?

indicators.note: the two parts are only slightly mixed, interlocked by swapping one letter across the join

parts.note: a ton is a heavy unit of weight
the answer to 12 across is LITTLE, and wee is the Scots word for little

explanation.surface: A heavyweight boxer mixing it with a little guy in town.
explanation.walkthrough: TON and WEE are run together and 'mixing it a bit' swaps the N and W where they meet.
explanation.definitionFit: A townee is a town-dweller, especially as opposed to a university student or a country person.

clue.text: Twist-in-the-tail Masefield work describing love bird

indicators.note: describing in the sense of drawing a line round, so one piece encloses another
only the tail of the poem title is twisted, so its last two letters change places

parts.note: Cargoes is a famous poem by John Masefield
love is zero in tennis, which looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: A Masefield piece with a twist ending, describing a lovebird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twist-in-the-tail' turns CARGOES into CARGOSE, which 'describing' wraps round O. The surface's 'love bird' splits: love is O, bird the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Cargoose is an old dialect name for the great crested grebe, a water bird.

clue.text: What will excite roadshow fan — I'm no promise-breaker

indicators.note: to excite is to stir up, so the answer is what stirs up into these letters, an anagram

explanation.surface: A fan of a TV roadshow declares themself trustworthy.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram is described backwards: the answer, stirred up, gives ROADSHOW FAN I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who never breaks a promise is reliable, a person who always keeps their pledges.

clue.text: Not much left and right to turn heads

indicators.note: the head of the word is turned round, its first two letters exchanging places

parts.note: a title is a legal right or claim, as to property

explanation.surface: An onlooker with little left to do but turn heads left and right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to turn heads' swaps the first two letters of TITLE, giving ITTLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A little is a small amount, so 'not much' can stand for it.

clue.text: Liquor drained with a cutting parting shot

indicators.note: parting means splitting apart, so the shot is split open to take the rest

parts.note: to have a go is to have a shot or attempt

indicators.note: cutting means slicing into, so the A goes inside

parts.note: all in means exhausted, completely drained

explanation.surface: A drinker, drained, cuts away with a parting shot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cutting' puts A in ALL IN to make ALLIAN; 'parting' splits GO round it.
explanation.definitionFit: Galliano is a sweet yellow Italian herbal liqueur, used in a Harvey Wallbanger.

clue.text: Irony etc. overturning outside a harbour

indicators.note: outside means one piece goes round the other
overturning means turning over, so the word is written backwards

parts.note: irony, metaphor and the like are tropes, figures of speech

explanation.surface: Irony and the like being overturned outside a harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overturning' makes SEPORT from TROPES, and 'outside' puts it round A.
explanation.definitionFit: A seaport is a coastal town or city with a harbour where ships dock.

clue.text: Starter against working under one well versed

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting one piece under another means it comes after it

parts.note: on can mean against, as leaning on or against a wall
I is the Roman numeral for one
on means working, as a machine that is switched on
so is a filler like well, as in 'so, what now?'
to be up on a subject is to be well versed in it

explanation.surface: A beginner set to work under one well-read person.
explanation.definitionFit: French onion soup is a classic first course served at the start of a meal.

clue.text: Having more excellence uncovered three times in the academic year?

indicators.note: uncovered means its outside letters are taken off, exposing the middle

parts.words: three times in the academic year
parts.note: with three terms in the academic year, three times a year is one a term

explanation.surface: Something done three times a year turns out better when unwrapped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uncovered' strips the first and last letters from ONE A TERM.
explanation.definitionFit: Neat can mean excellent or very good, as in 'that's neat', so the comparative means more so.

clue.text: 'To the West, no thanks' — independent Chinese 14

indicators.note: in an across clue, going west means reading right to left, so the word is turned round

parts.note: nay is an old word for no, as in a vote
ta is British informal for thanks

explanation.surface: An independent declines the offer to head west.
explanation.walkthrough: '14' points to SEAPORT, the answer to 14 across.
explanation.definitionFit: Yantai is a port city in Shandong province in eastern China.

clue.text: Surrounded by auxiliaries, spy chief's kept time

indicators.note: kept as in held, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: aids are auxiliaries or helpers
M is the head of MI6 in the James Bond stories; the 's stands for has

explanation.surface: A spy chief held by auxiliary staff, kept for a while.
explanation.definitionFit: Amidst is a preposition meaning in the middle of, so surrounded by.

clue.text: Audible relief on return, clearly preferred to one writer

indicators.note: something preferred to another takes its place, so one piece swaps in for another
on return means going back, so the word is written in reverse

parts.note: a sigh of relief is relief you can hear
I is the Roman numeral for one
well can mean clearly or skilfully, as in 'see well'

explanation.surface: A writer relieved on coming home, clearly favoured over another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on return' turns SIGH into HGIS; 'preferred to one' swaps WELL in for its I.
explanation.definitionFit: H. G. Wells was the English novelist who wrote The War of the Worlds and The Time Machine.

clue.text: See 11
Just a 12 fly trapped in tin

indicators.note: trapped in means held inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: Sn is the chemical symbol for tin
a midge is a small fly

explanation.surface: Just one little fly caught inside a tin.
explanation.walkthrough: '12' refers to LITTLE, the answer to 12 across.
explanation.definitionFit: A smidgen is a tiny amount, just a little bit of something.

clue.text: Has other ideas involving dessert wines new ewer decanted

indicators.note: involving here means mixing up, so the letters of dessert wines are rearranged
new means a fresh arrangement of the letters of ewer
decanted means poured out, so those letters are taken away

explanation.surface: Someone disagrees about pouring dessert wines from a new jug.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: the letters of DESSERT WINES, minus those of EWER (jumbled, 'new', and 'decanted'), give the answer rearranged ('involving').
explanation.definitionFit: To dissent is to disagree or hold a different opinion from others.

clue.text: Doubly striking ensemble

parts.note: doubly says two words for striking are wanted; the first is out, as workers on strike are
fit is British slang for attractive, so eye-catching or striking

explanation.surface: A doubly eye-catching ensemble.
explanation.walkthrough: Doubly means two different words for striking are joined: OUT, as workers on strike, and FIT, British slang for good-looking.
explanation.definitionFit: An outfit is a set of clothes worn together, i.e. an ensemble.

clue.text: See 7
Euphoria at opening Mr Kipling product, tucking into very good cakes and turnovers?

indicators.note: at opening points to the first letter of the word that comes before it
tucking into means being put inside something

parts.note: so can mean very good, as in the cheer 'so good'
Kim is a novel by Rudyard Kipling
rolls such as Swiss rolls are cakes

explanation.surface: Euphoria on opening a box of Mr Kipling's exceedingly good cakes.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Kipling is a British cake brand sold as exceedingly good cakes, but here he is the author Rudyard Kipling, whose novel is the product.
explanation.definitionFit: An Eskimo roll is a kayaking manoeuvre that flips the boat over and back upright, so a turnover.

clue.text: Is not half overwhelmed by upset we ought to overcome

indicators.note: overwhelmed by means swamped, so one piece is placed inside another
upset means knocked over, so the letters are thrown into a new order
not half means only half of the word is kept, its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone is half-swamped by the upset of what we should conquer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns WE OUGHT into OUTWEGH, and 'overwhelmed by' puts I, half of IS, inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To outweigh something is to surpass it in importance, so to overcome or prevail over it.

clue.text: Pottery school in the Home Counties

indicators.note: in means one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: SE, south-east England, where the Home Counties surround London
a pod is a school of whales or dolphins

explanation.surface: A pottery school based near London.
explanation.walkthrough: The Home Counties are the counties around London.
explanation.definitionFit: Spode is a famous brand of English porcelain and pottery from Stoke-on-Trent.

clue.text: Position of Goya's anagram

indicators.note: of means taken from within, so the letters lie inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: Where something stands in relation to an anagram of Goya.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface wants YOGA, an anagram of Goya, which is apt: the answer is a yoga pose.
explanation.definitionFit: An asana is a posture held in yoga practice.
